content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published guidelines on syphilis screening and treatment for pregnant women, emphasizing the importance of addressing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) as a significant global public health issue. These infections not only affect quality of life but also contribute to severe morbidity and mortality. STIs have direct consequences on reproductive and child health, including infertility, cancers, and pregnancy complications, and indirectly facilitate the sexual transmission of HIV, impacting both national and individual economies. Syphilis, caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum, is a bacterial STI that leads to substantial morbidity and mortality. It is transmitted through sexual contact with infectious lesions, blood transfusion, or transplacentally from a pregnant woman to her fetus. Congenital syphilis, resulting from mother-to-child transmission, can have devastating effects on the fetus if maternal infection is not detected and treated early in pregnancy. In 2012, syphilis was estimated to cause 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes globally, including 143,000 stillbirths, 62,000 neonatal deaths, 44,000 preterm or low-birth-weight infants, and 102,000 infected newborns. Early treatment of maternal syphilis can prevent these outcomes, with minimal risk to the fetus if the mother receives adequate treatment before the second trimester. The WHO guidelines recommend screening all pregnant women for syphilis during their first antenatal care visit. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. In settings with low syphilis screening coverage, high loss to follow-up, or limited laboratory capacity, on-site rapid testing strategies are suggested over standard off-site laboratory-based screening. In low-prevalence settings (syphilis prevalence below 5%), a single on-site rapid syphilis test (RST) is preferred. In high-prevalence settings (5% or greater), a combination of on-site RST followed by treatment and confirmatory rapid plasma reagin (RPR) testing is recommended. Treatment for syphilis in pregnant women involves benzathine penicillin, administered intramuscularly. If penicillin is unavailable, alternative antibiotics such as erythromycin or azithromycin may be used cautiously, though these do not cross the placental barrier completely, necessitating treatment of the newborn after delivery. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy. The guidelines emphasize the importance of timely and appropriate treatment to minimize adverse outcomes. The rationale for these updated guidelines stems from changes in STI epidemiology and advancements in prevention, diagnosis, and treatment since the previous WHO guidelines in 2003. The global burden of STIs remains high, with more than a million curable infections acquired daily. In 2012, there were an estimated 6 million new cases of syphilis among adults aged 15–49 years. Untreated STIs can lead to severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, and congenital infections. The guidelines also address the growing challenge of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in STIs, particularly for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Effective treatment protocols that consider global and local resistance patterns are essential to reduce the risk of further AMR development. The WHO emphasizes the need for countries to adopt updated global guidance and adapt it to their local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data. In summary, the WHO guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations for syphilis screening and treatment in pregnant women, aiming to reduce the burden of congenital syphilis and improve maternal and child health outcomes. These guidelines are part of a broader effort to strengthen STI prevention, diagnosis, and treatment globally.
